document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
enforcement_categories: Financial Penalties | Conformity Assessment | Market Surveillance
applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
implementation_notes: Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider duty; not applicable to deployers or to AI systems that are not high-risk.

document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
responsible_party: Developer and deployer ('any person involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India')
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certifications, internal policies, committee hearings, §2.5, PDF p. 33; peer monitoring and third-party audits, §2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).
enforcement_categories: Voluntary or Soft Accountability | Monitoring and Reporting
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: COMMITMENT: voluntary transparency reports by developers/deployers; MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). IMPLEMENTATION: no MeitY compliance schedule or transparency-reporting template found as of 25 Nov 2026. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; check indiaai.gov.in and meity.gov.in.

document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
responsible_party: Government (MeitY and sectoral regulators) to clarify and impose obligations; the eventual duty-bearers would be developers, deployers and end-users
responsibility_categories: Government | Regulator | Developer | AI Deployer | End User
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).
enforcement_categories: No Specific Mechanism Identified | Proposed or Future Mechanism
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: COMMITMENT: clarify how value-chain actors are governed and impose proportionate obligations; Action Plan: 'Develop clear liability regimes' (short term). IMPLEMENTATION: no liability regime or AI-specific obligations enacted. Secondary reports (Business Standard, Apr 2026; Economic Times via letsdatascience, Jul 2026) say AIGEG may push a unified legal framework and that MeitY is weighing a risk-based AI law. That would contradict the Guidelines' position that no separate AI law is needed. Unconfirmed; check for a draft bill. Sources: https://www.business-standard.com/industry/news/govt-body-plans-legal-framework-for-ai-companies-tech-oversight-126042001135_1.html ; https://letsdatascience.com/news/india-weighs-dedicated-risk-based-ai-regulation-af49db26

responsible_party: Government (developing body not named in the provision; Action Plan says 'with sectoral inputs'; AISI's listed functions include risk analysis)
enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: related sector-specific instrument. COMMITMENT: an India-specific, economy-wide risk assessment and classification framework (short-term action). IMPLEMENTATION: no general MeitY framework found. RELATED: CERT-In issued 'AI Security Auditing Guidelines' v1.0 (CISG-2026-04) on 4 Nov 2026, with a four-tier risk classification (Low, Moderate, High, Critical) that sets audit depth and frequency (secondary reports). That instrument covers security auditing, not the general framework recommended. Its legal force (guideline vs binding direction) needs verification from the CERT-In text; it is a candidate for a new IND record. PSA's office published a white paper (Jan 2026) proposing a national AI incidents database; no launch found. responsible_party: AI Safety Institute (IndiaAI Safety Institute), working with agencies and sectoral regulators
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified. AISI's role is research, testing and advice; the Guidelines give it no powers to compel testing or impose sanctions. It provides risk assessments and 'updates on industry compliance' to TPEC and AIGG (PDF p. 38).
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: institution exists; testing function not verified. COMMITMENT: AISI should test and evaluate AI systems and be adequately resourced. document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
responsible_party: Sectoral regulators and agencies (e.g. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI, ICMR, NHA, ministries), with MeitY as nodal ministry and AIGG coordinating
enforcement_mechanism: Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. The institutional framework maps regulators to 'Enforcing applicable laws and regulations', 'Supervising compliance' and 'Handling grievances' (PDF pp. 42-43). AIGG is to 'issue guidelines to ensure that firms are held accountable for compliance with local laws' (PDF p. 36).
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: coordinating body established in modified form. COMMITMENT: sectoral regulators enforce within their domains; new AIGG chaired by the PSA, including regulators (TRAI, CCI, DPB, RBI, SEBI etc.), supported by TPEC. The Guidelines describe that composition as 'illustrative and subject to periodic reviews' (PDF p. 37), so the membership differences below are a departure from a suggestion, not from a fixed design. IMPLEMENTATION: MeitY Office Memorandum of 13 Apr 2026 constituted the AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG), merging the proposed AIGG with the Economic Survey's AI Economic Council. It is chaired by the Minister of Electronics & IT (not the PSA), and none of RBI, SEBI, TRAI, CCI or DPB is a member. Its ToR repeat the Guidelines' AIGG functions and add labour-market tasks. It has no enforcement powers; it was created by an administrative memorandum, not a statute. TPEC constituted (NeGD release, May 2026). Sectoral enforcement continues under existing statutes; no change found. Sources: https://d12aarmt01l54a.cloudfront.net/cms/files/constitution-of-aigeg/1776346498.pdf ; https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2252739 ; https://negd.gov.in/?p=12809

document: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, as amended by the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 120(E), 10 February 2026)
responsible_party: Intermediaries offering a computer resource that enables the creation, modification or dissemination of synthetically generated information; significant social media intermediaries (rule 4(1A))
enforcement_mechanism: Due-diligence obligation under the IT Rules: under rule 7, if an intermediary fails to observe the Rules, 'the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 79 of the Act shall not be applicable to such intermediary' (loss of safe-harbour protection), exposing it to liability under the IT Act and other law. Takedown and blocking powers under the IT Act also apply.
applicability_status: In force (from 20 February 2026)
implementation_notes: Legally in force from 20 February 2026; MeitY issued FAQs on 10 February 2026 and prepared a further amendment in April 2026 on label display. Platform-level compliance has not been assessed, so the provision is coded as partially implemented rather than implemented.

applicability_status: In force (from 20 February 2026)
implementation_notes: No published enforcement action under the 2026 SGI duties was assessed for this study.

document: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (DSIT White Paper, CP 815, March 2023; amended version)
responsible_party: Regulatory authority (implementation through guidance); AI life cycle actors (may be asked by regulators to provide information)
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).
enforcement_categories: Existing Regulatory Powers | Monitoring and Evaluation
applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: non-statutory. COMMITMENT (2023): regulators apply the principle, supported by central guidance. IMPLEMENTATION: the Feb 2024 government response published 'Implementing the UK's AI regulatory principles: initial guidance for regulators' (6 Feb 2024). Ministers asked key regulators for their strategic approaches to AI, which DSIT published on 1 May 2024. The principle remains non-statutory; no standalone UK AI legislation found (law-firm trackers, 2025-2026). Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-the-uks-ai-regulatory-principles-initial-guidance-for-regulators ; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/regulators-strategic-approaches-to-ai/regulators-strategic-approaches-to-ai
